sections.report:
I've checked the heatmap closely. Here are my working notes, then the report.

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the dark weekday-morning block in the heatmap, then goes to the title, then to the big numbers on the right. It reads as a calm, tidy support-desk report about when tickets arrive. Assumed job: a support lead decides when to staff. The whole piece: 8 lines. One-sentence purpose yes; image and headline one idea yes; every element does a job yes; unity yes; copy finished yes; consistency yes; mood yes; headings name their sections yes. Outside the checklist: the "Busiest hour, weekdays 10:00" number contradicts the chart, and it isn't clear which dates "3,412" covers.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None. Every line in this section is yes.

Two things outside this section's lines, for the director. The first probably belongs under the data section.

1. **The headline number contradicts the chart** (no checklist line here; probably Charts and data). The stat "Busiest hour, weekdays **10:00**" is at about x 1034–1180, y 315–375. In the heatmap the 11:00 column (x ≈ 506–542) is the darkest every weekday. It reaches 30+ on Mon and Fri (y ≈ 212–248 and 364–400) and is 25–29 on Tue to Thu. The 10:00 column (x ≈ 468–504) is 25–29 on all five days. So 11:00 is at least as busy as 10:00 on every weekday, and busier on two. A viewer who compares the number with the darkest cells sees a mismatch. That makes them doubt both the stat and the chart, and this is a staffing decision. The cause could be the data, the stat, or the hour labels (each label sits at the left edge of its column, so a viewer may be one column off). Fix: make the stat and the chart agree. Either correct the stat, or label each column clearly as "10:00–11:00", or mark the busiest column on the chart. Defect. Weight: major. It is the one claim the page states outright, and the chart disproves it.
2. **"New tickets, September 3,412" doesn't say which dates it covers** (copy, no checklist line). It's at x 1034–1180, y 212–278. The subtitle says the chart covers "1 to 28 September", but the stat says "September". A stranger can't tell whether 3,412 counts 28 days or 30, or whether "Up 4% on August" compares equal periods. Fix: give the stat the same date range as the chart, or say "September (full month)". Defect, in copy. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The page holds together as one thing. It uses one blue ramp, one typeface, one heading, one chart with a summary column, and a source note. The nav, chart and stats look like one system, nothing is decorative, and the calm blue suits an operational report.
- The headline "When new tickets arrive" names exactly what the page answers. The subtitle then pins down the measure, scope and period ("per hour of the day, all queues, average week, 1 to 28 September"). The footnote rules out the obvious misreading ("when a ticket was opened, not when it was answered"). A first-time viewer can say what the page is for in one sentence.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The page title "When new tickets arrive" (x40–370, y95–125, about 28 px bold, near-black) and the three summary figures "3,412", "10:00" and "42 min" (x1034–1130, y230–450, about 26 px bold, near-black) look almost the same size, weight and color. The viewer can't tell whether the figures are headings of the same rank as the title or a separate tier of data. After the title, the eye gets pulled right to the column of figures before it reads the subtitle and the heatmap the page is about. Three bold numbers at title strength stacked together also pull hard on the eye. Why: two things that are meant to differ need a difference that is obvious at a glance, and a size only a step or two away reads as an accident (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8; Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale"). Fix: make the difference obvious in one direction. Either make the title clearly larger than the figures, or bring the figures down a clear step (or make them lighter or a muted color) so they read as a supporting tier under the title and the chart. Mark: convention. Weight: minor. The heatmap still clearly dominates, so the page works, but the reading order is less clean than it should be.

**What's working.**
- The heatmap's dark block of weekday cells from 09:00 to 16:00 (x430–730, y212–400) is by far the heaviest, highest-contrast mass on the page. The eye goes straight to the answer the title asks ("when do tickets arrive?") without any help from the text, so the chart does the work.
- The levels use more than size. The bold dark title sits over a regular grey subtitle, and each summary block goes from a small grey label to a big bold figure to a small grey note. Each level differs in weight and color as well as size, so even close sizes elsewhere (brand name, nav, subtitle) stay apart.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no two sizes almost the same)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes), Arrangement and space.** The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. The crop script could not run because Bash is denied.

First read: the eye lands on the dark blue band from 10:00 to 11:00 on Mon and Fri. It moves up to the title, then right to the "3,412" and "10:00" figures. This looks like a support-desk analytics report for a team lead. It feels calm and orderly.

1. One grid: yes. The logo, title, subtitle and source all start at x≈40. The heatmap, the legend label and the hour labels start at x≈88. The legend swatches start at x≈278, which is exactly the sixth column of the heatmap. The heatmap cells have an even 38 px pitch. The stats column starts at x≈1034, with its three blocks evenly spaced about 96 px apart.
2. Exact alignment, no near-misses: yes. The day labels are right-aligned to about x 78, just in front of the grid. The first stats label lines up with the top of the grid at about y 212–219. The stats column (about 212–470) matches the height of the heatmap (212–476).
3. Baselines across columns: yes. The stats column and the heatmap rows don't claim a shared baseline, and nothing reads as a mismatch.
4. Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes. Title and subtitle are tight, with a bigger gap before the chart. Inside each stat, label, number and change are tight, with about 45 px between stats. Hour labels sit close to the grid, and the legend sits about 28 px below it.
5. One group per box: yes. There are no boxes apart from the header rule.
6. No accidental groups: yes.
7. Nothing touching or overlapping: yes.
8. Margin from the page edge: yes. There's 40 px on the left, and the content ends about 100 px from the right edge.
9. Empty space gathered: yes. It sits in one band below y≈590 and one strip on the right.
10. Balance: yes. The blue mass sits centre-left and the stats column balances it on the right.
11. Centring by habit: yes. Everything is flush left, with no default centring.
12. Proportion: yes. The chart and side column split looks fine for a report screen.
13. Eye path: yes. The eye goes title → heatmap peak → stats → legend → source, and nothing leads it off the edge.

I answered no line `no` or `unsure`, so there were no reference entries to open.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The stats column is cut to the heatmap's frame.** It starts level with the top row of the grid (about y 212) and ends level with the Sun row (about y 470). Its three stats are evenly spaced about 96 px apart. The side figures look like part of the same report rather than a widget stuck on, and the eye moves from the 10:00 peak in the grid to the "10:00" figure in one step. Keep this alignment if the column gets more stats or the chart changes height.
- **The page uses two left edges and the legend follows the grid.** The outer edge at x 40 holds the logo, title, subtitle and source. The inner edge at x 88 holds the heatmap, hour labels and legend label. The legend swatches start exactly on the sixth heatmap column (x 278). So the page reads as one built block: text hangs on the outer edge, the chart sits on the inner one, and the day labels fill the space between, right-aligned to the grid.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**First read.** The eye lands on the heading "When new tickets arrive", drops to the dark band in the heatmap from 09:00 to 16:00 on weekdays, then moves right to the three big numbers. It reads as a reporting page in a help-desk tool, made for a support lead planning staff rotas. The text is quiet and orderly, and it stays out of the chart's way.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None. I answered yes to every line I could judge. One line is still open (see below). The crop script could not be run because Bash was denied, so I worked from the whole image at 1280 px wide.

Two things the checklist has no line for, which the director may want:
- **Copy, a number that can be read two ways.** The right-hand column (x≈1034, y≈219) says "New tickets, September 3,412". The subtitle says the data covers "1 to 28 September". A reader can't tell whether 3,412 is the whole month or only the 28 days shown, so it may not match the heatmap. "Up 4% on August" also leaves open whether August was a full month or 28 days. This is a defect, because people quote and compare a headline count, and the wrong reading changes how they see the trend. Minor. Fix: put the period in the label, e.g. "New tickets, 1–28 Sep", and compare against a period of the same length.
- **Type scale, two sizes too close.** The heading "When new tickets arrive" (~28 px) and the stat numbers "3,412 / 10:00 / 42 min" (~26 px bold) look only a couple of pixels apart, so the stats compete with the title for first place. I count about five sizes: ~28, ~26, ~16–17, ~13 and ~12. Taste, citing Bringhurst on sizes a few points apart. Minor. Fix: make the stat numbers clearly smaller than the heading, or make the heading clearly larger, so each has its own level. This belongs mainly to Hierarchy, so I'm leaving it to that critic.

**What's working.**
- **The source line (y≈573) makes the hours unambiguous.** It names the source and says "times in the support team's local time" and "when a ticket was opened, not when it was answered". Those are the two misreadings a staffing chart invites. It also adds what each fact means for the reader, which is what turns a source line into something people actually use.
- **One sans-serif family with a tight set of jobs.** Each element uses one change only: the bold heading, grey regular for the subtitle and labels, and bold numbers with small grey labels above and below them. The legend uses true en dashes ("0–4", "10–14"). The text looks finished without anything showing off.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The apostrophe in "team's" on the source line (≈x 640, y 573). It's too small to tell curly from straight at this resolution, and I couldn't make a zoomed crop. Check it in the live page or the source.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 unsure (curly quotes: apostrophe in the source line too small to tell)

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the dark-blue band of the heatmap at about Mon to Fri, 10:00 to 12:00, then goes to the title, then to the three numbers on the right. It reads as a support-desk report on when tickets come in, for team leads planning staffing. It feels calm and orderly. Assumed job: show leads at a glance when ticket load peaks, so they can staff for it. I could not run the crop script because Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image, which is about one screen (1280×800).

Color, judged outside the chart:
- Small palette: yes. Grays plus one blue ramp.
- Strong color kept to a small share of the area: yes.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Everything is cool, and nothing needs to come forward through temperature.
- Matching colors look the same everywhere: yes.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes.
- Dark theme background: yes (light theme, so it doesn't apply).

---

**Section.** Color: applies. Most of the color sits in the heatmap, which belongs under "Charts and data". This section covers the page around it: nav, title, KPI column, legend label and source line.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One hue on neutrals.** The page uses gray text and white backgrounds, and the blue appears only where the data is. All the color on the page means something, and the darkest cells (about x 505–543 and 640–656, Mon to Fri) are the only strong marks, so the eye goes straight to the weekday late-morning peak. The ramp also runs from light to dark in even steps, so the page would still read in grayscale.
- **No status color on the KPI changes.** "Up 4% on August" and "Down 6 min on August" are plain gray text with no red or green. "Up" for ticket volume and "down" for reply time could each be read as good or bad, so leaving them neutral avoids signalling a judgment the data doesn't make. The words carry the direction.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The screen has no photos, illustrations, icons, or graphic marks. The heatmap is a chart and belongs under Charts and data. "Northlight Desk" at about (40, 17)–(178, 37) is a plain bold wordmark set in the UI font, so it falls under Text.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. The piece is a day-by-hour heatmap of new tickets with three headline numbers beside it.

**Findings**
1. **No checklist line covers this: the "Busiest hour, weekdays: 10:00" number contradicts the chart.** On the right of the chart, at about x 1034–1180, y 315–375, the panel says 10:00. In the heatmap, the cells are about 38 px wide starting at x≈88. The two darkest cells (30+, Mon and Fri, at about x 506–542) fall in the 11:00 column, just left of the "12:00" label. The 10:00 column is 25–29 on every weekday, and 11:00 is the same shade or darker on each weekday. A viewer who checks the number against the chart finds they disagree. Then they can't trust either one, and the busiest hour is the fact a staffing decision would rest on. Possible causes: the stat is wrong, the hour labels are off by one, or the stat compares exact values that the 5-ticket bins hide. Fix direction: make the stat and the chart agree. If 10:00 really is busiest by exact count, say how it was worked out ("highest weekday average, 10:00–11:00"). Also make clear whether each hour label marks a column or a boundary. Each label is about as wide as one cell, so it reads either way. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No. The heading at about x 40–370, y 95–125 reads "When new tickets arrive", and the subtitle describes the data's scope. Neither says what the chart shows: tickets cluster from about 09:00 to 16:00 on weekdays, peak in late morning, and weekends are light. Everything needed to read the chart is there, but the viewer has to find the pattern alone, and only the side panel hints at it. Fix direction: make the heading the finding, for example "Most tickets arrive weekday mornings, peaking late morning". Its hour must match whatever finding 1 settles on. Taste (common sense; the catalog entry has no approved source). Weight: minor, because the chart pattern is strong enough that most viewers get it in a glance.
3. **No checklist line covers this: the periods behind "New tickets, September: 3,412 / Up 4% on August" are unclear.** The chart covers 1 to 28 September, but the stat says "September", and August has 31 days. A viewer can't tell whether 3,412 is 28 days or 30, or whether "up 4%" compares totals or a daily rate. With unequal periods, a total could be up while the daily rate is down. Fix direction: give the stat's date range, or compare per-day rates. Defect (it is a number viewers act on). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The palette is a single blue going from light to dark in seven labelled bins of even width. The order of the shades follows the order of the values, it still reads without colour vision, and the empty night hours fade back so the weekday block stands out at once.
- Each headline number has its comparison right under it ("Up 4% on August", "Same as August", "Down 6 min on August"). The viewer can judge good or bad without looking anywhere else.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 15 yes, 1 no (title states the finding)

I critiqued only and changed no files. Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I worked from the whole image, which fits on one screen, and read the entries directly from `references/ux.md`.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The controls are the top nav links (Queues, Agents, Reports, Settings); there are no buttons, fields or dialogs.

**Findings**
1. **"Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?"**: No. The report is fixed to the scope its subtitle states (x≈40–625, y≈140–157): "all queues, average week, 1 to 28 September". Nowhere near the title or the heatmap (x≈88–998, y≈212–476) is there a date range picker, a queue filter, or an export.
   - **What the viewer meets:** A support lead who staffs by queue, or wants to compare with August, sees one fixed view. The page already compares with August in the KPI column ("Up 4% on August", "Same as August"), which invites the question "show me August". The page can't answer it, so the lead has to ask someone or look elsewhere.
   - **Why:** Nielsen 7, Flexibility and efficiency of use: frequent actions such as filters get shortcuts that don't get in the way of novices.
   - **Fix direction:** Put a compact period control and a queue filter in one row between the subtitle and the chart. Default them to the current scope so first-time readers see the same page as now, and add an export there if leads share these.
   - **Kind:** Convention. **Weight:** Minor. The page still answers its main question, when tickets arrive, without these controls.

**What's working.**
- **Current page is marked.** Reports is bold in the nav while its siblings are regular grey, and the page title names the report. You know where you are at once, with one plain cue, which is exactly what the approved fix for Nielsen 1 asks for.
- **Help sits where it's needed.** The source line at y≈573 says the hours are in the support team's local time and count when a ticket was opened, not answered. That heads off the most likely misreading of a staffing chart, right under the chart.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the nav links show a visible focus ring for keyboard users.
- Whether the heatmap cells give exact counts on hover or focus. The legend bins (0–4 … 30+) are the only way to read values here, so exact counts on hover would matter for planning.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions: no date or queue filter on a fixed-scope report), 1 unsure (focus indicator at least 2 px with 3:1 contrast)
